title: Encoding, hashing, encryption, signing
summary: The four operations everyone mixes up, told apart by two questions: is there a key, and can it be reversed?

steps.title: Two questions sort everything
body: Ask of any operation: **does it need a secret?** and **can you get the input back?**
| Operation | Secret needed? | Reversible? | Example | Purpose |
| **Encoding** | no | yes, by anyone | Base64, hex, UTF-8 | make bytes fit a text channel |
| **Hashing** | no | no | SHA-256 | fingerprint; detect change |
| **Encryption** | yes (key) | yes, with the key | AES-GCM | hide content |
| **Signing / MAC** | yes (key) | not the point: output is a *tag* next to the data | ECDSA, HMAC | prove origin and integrity |

The classic bug: treating **encoding** as protection. A Base64 "secret" in a config file, a "hashed" password that is really Base64, a JWT payload someone thinks is encrypted. Base64 hides data from nobody.

steps.explain: No key, no secret: anyone can decode Base64. It is a way to *carry* bytes, not to *hide* them.

steps.prompt: Sort each by what it actually is.
steps.explain: Encodings have no key. Hashes have no key and no way back. Ciphers have a key and a way back. MACs and signatures have a key and produce a tag.

steps.prompt: A JWT's middle part decodes to `{"sub":"ada","role":"admin"}` with a Base64 decoder. What protects that payload from being *read*?
options: Nothing: a signed JWT is readable by anyone, the signature only stops changes
steps.explain: Signing gives integrity and authenticity, not confidentiality. The *Authentication & JWT* topic (JWT in depth) builds this by hand; here the point is the category: signed is not encrypted.

steps.title: Hashing is one-way, encryption is two-way
body: byte[] digest = SHA256.HashData(data);          // no key; cannot be undone
byte[] tag    = HMACSHA256.HashData(key, data); // key; proves who made it

A hash cannot be "decrypted": there is no key, and many inputs map to each output. When someone says they "decrypted a hash", they *guessed* inputs until one matched. That is why short, guessable inputs (passwords, phone numbers) are not protected by a plain hash at all; module 2 covers what to do instead.

steps.prompt: A support ticket says: "Please decrypt the SHA-256 of the customer's email so we can contact them." What is the honest answer?
options: It cannot be decrypted; the only route is guessing emails and hashing each one
Run SHA-256 again to reverse it
steps.explain: A hash has no inverse and no key. If guessing works (emails are guessable!), the hash was never protecting much.

steps.prompt: Complete the code so each line does what its comment says.
code: string carried = Convert.__1__(data);               // encoding: fit bytes into text
byte[] digest = __2__.HashData(data);               // hashing: fingerprint, no key
byte[] tag = __3__.HashData(key, data);             // MAC: needs the key
steps.explain: Base64 is the encoding, SHA-256 the hash, and HMAC-SHA256 the keyed tag. Only the last one needed a secret.

steps.prompt: Match each requirement to the operation that meets it.
pairs: Put a binary image inside a JSON string
Detect that a downloaded file was corrupted
Store a national ID so only the app can read it back
Prove a webhook came from the provider you share a key with
Let anyone check a software release came from the vendor
steps.explain: The last two differ in who can check: a MAC needs the shared secret, a signature only needs the public key.

steps.title: Three operations side by side
prompt: - `string Encode(string text)`: the Base64 of the UTF-8 bytes.
- `string Hash(string text)`: lowercase hex SHA-256 of the UTF-8 bytes.
- `string Mac(string key, string text)`: lowercase hex HMAC-SHA256, with the UTF-8 bytes of `key` as the key.
The tests check the properties that tell them apart: Encode is reversible by anyone, Hash is fixed for the same text, and Mac changes when the key changes.
template: Dojo.Eq("Mac(\"key\", quick brown fox)", "f7bc83f430538424b13298e6aa6fb143ef4d59a14946175997479dbc2d1a3cd8", Mac("key", "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog"));
Dojo.Check("a different key gives a different tag", Mac("key1", "x") != Mac("key2", "x"), "same tag for two keys");
hints: Turn each string into bytes with `Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes` and each digest into text with `Convert.ToHexStringLower`.
